title: Tenant-aware OTLP relay with sampling translation and rate-limit mapping
creator: Aisha Kaur
description:
Problem: We currently push raw OTLP spans from edge collectors directly to several backend stores with different ingestion expectations. This leads to per-tenant overages, inconsistent sampling semantics across backends, and a lack of tenant-aware rate shaping. Goal: Implement a lightweight, tenant-aware OTLP relay service that: 1) translates and normalizes incoming OTLP traces into backend-specific payloads (Jaeger/Tempo-compatible and native OTLP variants), 2) enforces per-tenant ingestion rate limits and burst policies, 3) translates sampling hints and legacy sampling attributes into consistent sampling_decision fields that downstream stores can honor, and 4) exposes mapping rules that can be updated dynamically without restarts.

Design sketch: - Relay runs as a horizontally scalable service in the observability cluster (k8s deployment). - Incoming spans annotated with tenant_id (x-redwood-tenant header) are routed to a per-tenant rule engine which applies:   * attribute normalization (rename legacy tags to standardized keys),   * sampling translation (e.g., convert custom sampler annotations into otel.sampling.priority / trace_flags),   * backend mapping (decide which backend to forward to based on tenant policy and SLOs). - Rate limiting: token-bucket per tenant with configurable steady-state QPS and burst capacity. Rate rules are expressed as a simple YAML stored in the config store (etcd) and cached in the relay; updates are hot-reloaded. - Backpressure and fallback: when a backend signals overload (5xx or high latency), the relay can perform configurable degradations: drop low-priority traces, fallback to a cheaper backend, or persist to a short-term buffer (S3/kafka) for async replay. - Observability: relay exports its own metrics (per-tenant ingest_qps, dropped_spans, translate_latency_ms), traces for relay processing, and a debug endpoint for rule inspection.

Acceptance criteria: - Relay accepts OTLP/gRPC and OTLP/HTTP from existing collectors with no collector changes required. - Per-tenant rate limits are enforced and observable; unit tests and load tests demonstrate limits under high QPS. - Sampling translation is reversible and validated: downstream spans contain expected sampling fields for three canonical cases (forced-sample, forced-drop, inherited). - Dynamic rule updates apply within 30s of config change without restart. - End-to-end tests proving that when primary backend returns 503, relay falls back to configured secondary and increments fallback counter. - Dashboard panels added to observability console: per-tenant ingest, drop-rate, translation latency, and fallback events.

Implementation plan (high level): - Week 1: protobuf definitions + skeleton relay service + local integration harness. - Week 2: implement attribute mapping and sampling translation logic + unit tests. - Week 3: implement per-tenant rate-limiter + e2e load tests (k6) against a fake backend. - Week 4: backend adapters (Jaeger/Tempo push paths), fallback buffer implementation, and metrics. - Week 5: rollout canary to internal tenants, monitor dashboards, iterate on edge cases.

Testing & validation: - Create a synthetic tenant generator to produce a mix of high-cardinality attributes and sampling scenarios. - Load test targets: sustained 10k reqs/s across cluster with 5% burst to validate token-bucket behaviour. - Integrate functional tests into CI that run translation unit tests and a small integration test using an in-memory backend.

Rollout and migration notes: - Start canary with non-production tenants and a narrow tenant allowlist. - Provide a compatibility mode where relay forwards unmodified payloads unless mapping rules exist for a tenant. - Add a one-week audit window during which we monitor dropped spans and fallback events; implement alert thresholds for unexpected drops.

Open questions / trade-offs: - Where to store dynamic rules: etcd vs ConfigService API. etcd gives lower latency but requires careful RBAC; ConfigService gives management UI. - How aggressive to be with fallback trimming vs buffering (cost trade-off). - Whether to implement cross-tenant batching optimizations in relay or defer to downstream collectors.
